cookieBanner.words: The banner ships in all 82 languages, so it speaks whichever language a visitor arrives in. Consent written in a language somebody cannot read is not consent at all, which is why this is not left to be filled in later.
cookieBanner.page: The banner links to /<language>/cookies — an ordinary static page of your project. Its text is edited in the code beside the page, like a blog post; ask your agent for the manage-cookie-banner skill.
cookieBanner.on: Visitors are asked for consent, and can change their answer from the footer.
cookieBanner.off: No consent strip and no footer button. Choose this for a private tool with no analytics.
cookieBanner.saved: Saved — applies on the next page load, no rebuild

visibility.intro: Everything on this page is already built and holding. It is here so you can see what your project does without you — and check any of it yourself.
visibility.searchBody: Multilingualism with modern search optimisation and an installable app is normally a long development cycle — and the one AI-written projects lose quietly: pages drift from prepared to recomputed, translations start reading as copies of each other, and half the languages never reach search results.
visibility.searchSignals: The language signals are in place on every public page: each one declares itself the original, names its translations for every language you enable, and adds x-default for visitors you do not cover. Without them a search engine reads translations as copies of one another and whole languages never reach results — the site meanwhile looks perfectly fine.
visibility.modelsBody: The same is true for the reader people remember last and who is already arriving: the model. It comes itself, reads, and retells your site in its own words — so the project publishes a machine map of itself and a clean markdown twin of every page, built from the same text, so the two can never drift.
visibility.appBody: Your site installs like an app: its own icon on the home screen, a launch without browser chrome, and pages already seen opening without a network. The offline copy never replaces the live site — pages always come from the network while it is there, so a text you change in the panel appears immediately.
visibility.mapsBody: Robots are answered by name — search crawlers and models separately — and every map is declared to them in the first file they open. The map lists your home page, catalogue, blog and each article in every enabled language; it never lists pages behind a login, which exist per visitor and would return a sign-in form to a crawler.
visibility.noJsBody: Pages arrive as finished HTML from the server, and links are ordinary links — so the site reads and navigates with scripts disabled. This is not an advantage over a dynamic application, and interactive parts do degrade; but if yours is an informational site, visitors can use it safely in any environment, including ones where scripts are blocked for them.
visibility.cost: Here it is built, tested many times over, and it holds under load at no extra server cost: a prepared page costs the same at a hundred visits and at a hundred thousand.
visibility.choice: So the only thing left for you is the choice of languages. Whichever you pick, nothing else here is left to build.
visibility.docSeoTitle: Search optimisation: what is already built
visibility.docAioTitle: AI optimisation: what is already built
visibility.docPwaTitle: Progressive web app: what is already built
visibility.docRobotsTitle: Rules for robots: what is already built
visibility.offlineHint: Pages the visitor has already opened work without a network. Turning this off does not merely stop installing it — it removes the worker from devices that already have it and clears its caches.
visibility.imagesBody: The page arrives with the picture already INSIDE it: a tiny blurred copy of the image, about 150 bytes, is written into the markup — no separate request for it, so the visitor sees the shape and colours of the coming image in the same millisecond as the heading. Its space is reserved in advance, from its real dimensions, so the text does not jump when the file lands. The real image follows and replaces the blurred one by itself.
visibility.imagesSpeed: This is not decoration but two of the three figures a search engine measures your page by: the layout jump as things load, and how fast the largest element on screen appears — most often that element is an image. Meanwhile a phone does not download a file made for a large monitor: the needed sizes are produced from one original on demand, the format is matched to the browser, and everything below the first screen loads only when the visitor reaches it. Works with JavaScript disabled.
visibility.coverAlt: Lighthouse report: one hundred out of one hundred for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO — beside this project catalogue
visibility.coverCaption: A real measurement of this project, not a marketing picture: 100 out of 100 across all four sections. On the left, the catalogue whose images came from the store.
visibility.dataBody: The project already has four stores, all on your server: rows, files, vector memory for search by meaning, and a knowledge graph for questions about connections. None of them needs to be started, configured or registered anywhere. You never design a schema: a new table is declared in one place and appears in every environment by itself — no migration files, no state where the server is ahead of your laptop.
visibility.dataCost: There is no step where free becomes paid and then becomes per-request-and-per-gigabyte. Data costs exactly what your server costs, however many queries it serves; a traffic spike turns into load on a processor you already paid for, not into an invoice. Outgrow it and you take a bigger server: the price rises linearly and the data travels with you, because it is files. And we spend that server carefully — public pages are prepared ahead and never query the database, answers are cached with a stated lifetime, a list is one query per page rather than one per row.
visibility.docDbTitle: The database: what is already built
visibility.docStorageTitle: Object storage: what is already built
visibility.docVectorsTitle: Vector memory: what is already built
visibility.docRagTitle: Agentic RAG: what is already built
visibility.authBody: Sign-in, accounts and access control work from the first minute and cost nothing: no cloud sign-in service to connect, no monthly fee per active user. Email and password work with no configuration; magic-link and Google sign-in are enabled by entering keys in the panel — the code is written. The library everything is built on supports over eighty providers: connecting one is an edit to a single file, by you or with our help.
visibility.authRoles: The most valuable part here is the least visible: roles are already attached to routes. To make a page available only to the right people you do not protect it — you build it on an existing route, and access lands with the holders of that role by itself. Four layers: personal account, staff, finance, administration; the first person to register receives every role at once. None of this costs speed: public pages are prepared ahead and never ask about sign-in.
visibility.designSystemBody: Nobody decides to make a site inconsistent — the drift accumulates one harmless edit at a time. A heading slightly larger here, a margin slightly tighter there, a card with a rounder corner on the third page. Each decision is reasonable on its own, and none of them looks like a mistake.
visibility.designSystemDrift: Then comes the part that matters for AI-assisted work: an agent reads the existing code as its example. While there is one way to describe a heading, it repeats that way. Once there are three, the agent draws a conclusion that is flawless from where it stands — there is no single rule here, so anything goes — and every new page adds a fourth. The more you build, the faster the drift. Here it is closed by primitives, tokens and four machine-checked laws that run inside the build: a violation does not reach the product, it stops the release.
visibility.docDesignSystemTitle: Design system: why the project does not drift apart
visibility.staticBody: Public pages are built ahead of time and served as files — with practically no load on the server. A dynamic page is recomputed on every visit: a multilingual site with a hundred pages and ten languages recalculates a thousand variants for every visitor, and growth in traffic turns into growth in the bill.
visibility.staticDrift: Static is much harder to build than dynamic, and the difficulty runs one way: any shortcut leads from static to dynamic, never back. Reading a cookie, a request header or a session check inside a layout turns the whole subtree dynamic — silently, without an error. A particular trap waits when private pages are added: since a dynamic layer now exists anyway, it feels simpler to make everything dynamic. Bills in the tens of thousands of dollars have grown from exactly a few such lines.
visibility.staticGuard: So the rule is held by a machine, not by an agreement. Public and private pages live in physically separate layers, and a check walks the entire public layer looking for signs of dynamics — on a match the build stops. Not a warning, not a log entry: the release does not happen until the violation is gone. A checklist is followed for as long as it is remembered; the first shortcut would bring dynamics back, and you would learn about it from the bill.
visibility.docStaticTitle: Static generation: the decision that costs the most

devTools.intro: These are the tools the project is BUILT with, not the ones that ship inside the product. They live on the developer's machine and never reach your visitor. The Tools section is about something else: ready-made pieces you can take into the application.
devTools.growing: The list will grow. Only what genuinely solves a task and has been proven in real work belongs here — not everything that can be installed.
devTools.browserBody: The Claude extension for Chrome gives the coding agent eyes: it opens a page in your browser and looks at the result of its own work. A whole class of defects cannot be found any other way — console errors, behaviour with scripts disabled, the service worker and offline, the page AFTER the code has run. In this project that is how nine errors on every page were found, and somebody else's error message standing in place of a video.
devTools.browserLimits: The boundaries are stated plainly: the agent never enters keys, passwords or payment details, never creates accounts or signs in to yours, never pays or accepts terms. So «make me an OAuth client in the Google console» or «set up Stripe» will not be done — that is your hand. It will walk you to the right screen, explain the fields, and verify the result after you enter it.

It is where you see the project as a whole — every file, every change, the difference before and after — and where Claude Code can live as an extension instead of a separate terminal window. This is the tool you cannot do without: without it the project stays a black box you can only ask about.

designFonts.intro: Three roles, one decision each: headings, body text, and monospace. The set opens on the system font — it downloads nothing and reaches no third party.

heading.label: Headings
heading.description: H1 through H4. This is where a project gets its character.

body.label: Body text
body.description: Paragraphs, lists, captions — most of what a person actually reads.

designFonts.systemNote: Takes whatever the device already has. Nothing is downloaded, nothing leaves the page, and text is visible in the very first frame.
designFonts.previewText: The quick brown fox — Съешь ещё этих мягких булок 0123
designFonts.helpLabel: About fonts: where they come from and how they are connected
designFonts.helpWhere: The families in this list come from Google Fonts (fonts.google.com), all under a free licence — OFL or Apache. The files themselves are NOT stored on your server: a visitor receives them from fonts.googleapis.com, whose cache is already warm on nearly every device.
designFonts.helpHow: Saving writes the family name and its stylesheet URL into DESIGN-CONFIG/design-config.json on your server. The application reads that file on every render and emits two things: a <link> to the stylesheet in <head>, and a CSS variable that the type primitive uses. A <link> rather than an @import on purpose — the browser sees a link immediately, while an @import inside <style> costs an extra network round-trip before the font is even requested. No rebuild is needed; the change shows on the next page load.
designFonts.helpPrivacy: Connecting an external font hands the visitor IP address to Google servers. A German court has ruled that this alone breaches GDPR (LG München I, 3 O 17493/20). The system option avoids the question entirely: it never reaches outside. If you need both a custom font and that guarantee, the font files have to be hosted on your own server — that is a separate step, not a setting.
designFonts.helpAlphabet: A font without Cyrillic turns a Russian page into a row of rectangles, and the build will not warn you — the page renders perfectly, it is simply unreadable. Every entry states which alphabets it covers; check it against the languages you switched on.
designFonts.helpSystemTitle: Why the system font is first.
designFonts.helpSystem: It is the fastest possible answer: nothing to download, nothing to wait for, no third party involved. For most projects it is also the right one — a custom font earns its cost only when the brand actually depends on it.

designType.intro: One number changes the whole set: headings, body text, captions — all of it, proportions intact.
designType.scaleHint: A multiplier over the project scale. 1.0 is the size the project ships with.
designType.leadingHint: The space between lines of body text. Lower is denser, higher is airier.
designType.previewBody: And this is body text underneath it — the size most of your visitors will actually read.
designType.helpLabel: Why one multiplier and not nine separate sizes
designType.helpWhyTitle: Nine fields are nine ways to break the scale.
designType.helpWhy: A subtitle larger than its heading, body text smaller than a caption — that is exactly the disarray this project spent a day removing from its code. A multiplier moves everything at once and keeps the proportions: the set is either bigger or smaller, never inconsistent.
designType.helpRange: Between 0.75 and 1.5. Outside it text is either unreadable or breaks the layout, and you would only discover that by opening every page. The limit lives in the application, not in this form — a value has to be checked where it arrives, not where it is typed.
designType.helpLive: The value is written into DESIGN-CONFIG on your server; the application reads it on every render as a CSS variable, and each step of the scale is calculated from it. The change shows on the next page load.

designShape.intro: Corners, borders and breathing room — the shape of every surface on the site.
designShape.radiusHint: Applies to cards, panels, buttons and inputs at once — each derives its own radius from this one value.
designShape.borderHint: A two-pixel border changes the character of an interface more than a colour does.
designShape.spaceHint: Vertical breathing room on every page. Content pages and work screens keep their difference — this moves both together.
designShape.widthHint: How wide the middle column of a page may grow. The header, the first screen and the footer are always full width.
designShape.previewBody: Its text sits inside the border, at the distance the density sets.
designShape.helpLabel: How these four values reach the pages
designShape.helpRadius: The project computes small, medium, large and extra-large corners from this single number, so a card, a button and an input never disagree. Setting them separately is how interfaces end up with three different corners on one screen.
designShape.helpSpaceTitle: Density is a multiplier, not a number of pixels.
designShape.helpSpace: Content pages are airier than work screens on purpose: one is read, the other is worked in. The multiplier moves both and keeps that difference — separate fields would let a work screen become airier than a content page, which is not a setting but a defect.
designShape.helpWidth: The page header, the first screen, the closing section and the footer are always full width. This value limits the column between them — the one the reader's eye travels along, where an over-long line becomes hard to follow.

designColors.intro: Seven roles, two themes. Each colour is an override: leave it untouched and the project theme decides.

primary.label: Brand colour
primary.description: Buttons, links, active states. The one colour a visitor will remember.

accent.label: Accent
accent.description: Highlights and hovers — a quieter relative of the brand colour.

muted.label: Muted surface
muted.description: Cards, panels, the background of secondary blocks.

border.label: Borders
border.description: Lines between elements — the quietest colour on the page.

designColors.contrastHint: Text against the page background. Below 4.5 the text fails the accessibility threshold for normal sizes.
designColors.previewBody: And the body text under it, in the colour people will actually read.
designColors.helpLabel: How colours reach the site, and what is computed for you
designColors.helpPairTitle: The text on a button is computed, not asked for.
designColors.helpPair: Every coloured role has a paired text colour on top of it. Change the brand colour and leave the pair alone, and a light brand colour keeps white text — a button whose label cannot be seen. The application derives that pair from the brightness of your colour, so the label stays readable whatever you pick.
designColors.helpThemesTitle: Light and dark are separate values.
designColors.helpThemes: A colour set once is almost always wrong on the other theme: dark text on a dark background disappears entirely. Set only the theme you care about — the other keeps the project's.
designColors.helpContrastTitle: The contrast figure is a measurement, not an opinion.
designColors.helpContrast: It is the ratio between text and background as the accessibility standard defines it. 4.5 is the threshold for normal text, 3.0 for large. Below that the page is not 'a matter of taste' — part of your visitors cannot read it.
designColors.schemesHint: One press sets all seven roles in both themes. Adjust anything afterwards — the change stays; press the same scheme again and its values come back.
designColors.schemeCustom: Your own combination — no ready-made scheme matches it exactly.

mapDesign.intro: Four decisions in the order they matter: the fonts first, then how big the text is, then the shape of surfaces, then colour. Each applies to the whole site at once.
mapDesign.allDefault: Nothing has been changed yet — the site looks the way the project theme decided, and that is a legitimate state, not an unfinished one.
mapDesign.liveNote: Every value on this page is read from the same file the site applies, so what you see here is what visitors see. Changes take effect on the next page load, without a rebuild.

fonts.title: Fonts — the voice of the product, and the first cost of loading
body: Three roles, not one font: headings, body text and monospace solve different problems, and folding them into a single field robs a product of its voice. The set opens on the system option, which takes the font already on the device — text is visible in the first frame and nothing leaves the page.

A catalogue instead of a text field removes three silent failures: a typo quietly falls back to the system font, a font without Cyrillic turns Russian text into rectangles, a forgotten URL leaves the name without the file. The build warns about none of them.

type.title: Typography — one multiplier instead of nine ways to break the scale
body: Text size is one number for the whole set: headings, body and captions move together and keep their proportions. Nine separate fields would look more generous and would let a subtitle grow larger than its heading.
This is not hypothetical: that exact disarray already existed here — nine different descriptions of a first-level heading — and removing it took a working day.

shape.title: Shapes and spacing — what reads as considered, or as rushed
body: One radius produces five: small, medium, large and extra-large are derived from it, so a card, a button and an input cannot disagree. Screens end up with three different corners exactly where each element decides for itself.

Density is a multiplier, not a pixel count: content pages are airier than work screens on purpose, and the multiplier moves both while keeping the difference. Width governs the middle of the page only — header, first screen and footer are always full width.

colors.title: Colours — ten ready schemes and a guard against the unreadable
body: A scheme sets all seven roles at once and in both themes: the visitor switches themes, so a decision describing only the light half would leave the dark one from the previous choice. Everything stays editable afterwards — your change lives on top of the scheme.

The label colour on a button is computed from the brightness of your colour, not asked for: otherwise a light brand colour would keep white text and produce a button whose label cannot be seen. Contrast is shown as a number while you choose — a measurement from the accessibility standard, not an opinion.

sections.title: Sections — reusable blocks of design
body: A page is assembled from sections — ready block kinds. A page material is data, not markup: the text lives separately and how it looks is the section decision. So a rule added to one kind reaches every page where that kind appears.
From this follows the point: the look of a project consists of exactly two things — the set of sections and the token values from the neighbouring pages. That is what makes a design portable.

SOON: importing ready section sets, and a page builder. The foundation already stands — a catalogue of twenty-one kinds, a machine check for specimens, and tokens that apply without a rebuild. No dates: a capability is announced once a check holds it.

media.helpLabel: Объектное хранилище — файлы в сравнении с базой данных
media.helpHolds: Сами файлы: изображения, видео, звук, документы. Байты, а не строки. Хранилище отдаёт их потоком, ставит заголовки кеширования, обрезает изображения и монтирует видео.

Это разделение не бюрократия: файлы внутри базы раздувают её и делают каждую резервную копию медленной, а факты, живущие только в файловой системе, нельзя ни искать, ни фильтровать, ни соединять. Каждое держит то, в чём сильно, и они указывают друг на друга.
media.helpCost: Диск, и больше ничего. Ни модели, ни оплаты за запрос — хранилище живёт на вашем сервере, поэтому файл, отданный миллион раз, стоит столько же, сколько отданный однажды.
